findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case sensitive, so the block list is trivially bypassed
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` looks the address up with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, an exact, case-sensitive comparison, and nothing in the model or the migration normalizes the stored address either. Sign-up emails are not downcased before validation (`User.new_from_params` assigns `params[:email]` verbatim), so an address blocked as `bad@spam.com` passes validation when submitted as `Bad@Spam.com`. The unique index on `blocked_emails.email` is also case sensitive, so duplicate case variants can be stored. Both the stored value and the lookup should be downcased (or the comparison made case-insensitive) for the feature to actually block anything.

findings.title: Match statistics written during validation are rolled back when the save fails
findings.body: `should_block?` performs `record.save` to bump `match_count`/`last_match_at`, and it is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, i.e. inside `User#save`'s validation step. ActiveRecord wraps `save` in a transaction and issues `ActiveRecord::Rollback` when validation returns false, so in the normal blocking path (validation fails → save returns false) the statistics update is rolled back and `match_count`/`last_match_at` are never persisted — exactly the case the model and `blocked_email_spec` claim to record. The counters should be updated outside the record's transaction (e.g. in a separate connection/`update_all` after validation, or from the controller) rather than as a side effect of a validator.

findings.title: Validator side effect causes match_count to be incremented more than once per signup
findings.body: `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which writes to the database. Validation is not idempotent for callers: `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), so the blocked-email counters are incremented twice for a single sign-up attempt, and any other code path that validates a user more than once inflates the counters further. Counting should happen once per attempt, outside the validation callback.

findings.title: Non-atomic match_count increment loses updates and silently ignores save failures
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1; record.save` is a read-modify-write: two concurrent sign-up attempts with the same blocked address both read the same value and write the same incremented value, so one match is lost. Additionally the return value of `save` is discarded, so a failed save (e.g. a validation error on a legacy row with a blank email) silently drops the statistics. Use an atomic SQL increment (`increment!`/`update_all("match_count = match_count + 1")`) instead.

findings.title: action_type is NOT NULL with no database default
findings.body: `action_type` is declared `null: false` without a default; the default value is only applied by the model's `before_validation :set_defaults`. The spec for this feature explicitly anticipates the table being "manually loaded with some emails" — any such bulk insert or raw SQL insert that omits `action_type` will fail with a NOT NULL violation. Adding `default: 1` (the `:block` value) to the column would make the intended default hold at the database level.

findings.title: Mutable array declared on the controller prototype is shared between instances
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` puts a single array object on the class prototype, so every instance created from `Discourse.CreateAccountController` mutates the same array via `pushObject`. If more than one instance is ever created (or the container is reset, e.g. in tests), rejected emails leak across instances and are never cleared. The array should be initialised per instance (e.g. in `init`) or stored as `null` and lazily created.

findings.title: Server-rejected email is reported to the user as "invalid"
findings.body: When an email is in `rejectedEmails` the field validation shows `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, i.e. the "email address is invalid" message, even though the server rejected it because it is blocked or already taken. After the flash message disappears the user is left with a message telling them their address is malformed, which will send them down the wrong path. The server-provided error message (`result.errors.email`) should be surfaced instead of a generic format error.

findings.title: New validator spec only covers the stubbed blocked-email branch
findings.body: The spec stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` entirely, so nothing exercises the real lookup (including the case-sensitivity problem), nothing verifies that a `User` with a blocked email actually fails to save, and the whitelist/blacklist branches that were moved out of `User#email_validator` into this new class have no coverage here. A regression in the moved whitelist/blacklist code or in the interaction between the validator and `BlockedEmail` would not be caught.
